name: Harriet Tubman
info: Harriet Tubman (c. 1822–1913) was an American abolitionist who escaped slavery in Maryland, led some 70 enslaved people to freedom on the Underground Railroad, served the Union Army as a scout and spy and campaigned for women's suffrage.

facts.born: c. March 1822 in Dorchester County, Maryland, into slavery, as Araminta "Minty" Ross; daughter of Harriet ("Rit") Green and Ben Ross, enslaved by the Brodess and Thompson families
facts.died: 10 March 1913, of pneumonia, in Auburn, New York, surrounded by friends and family; buried with semi-military honours at Fort Hill Cemetery in Auburn
facts.role: Conductor on the Underground Railroad (1850s); cook, nurse, scout and spy for the Union Army (1862–1865); suffragist; founder of the Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged in Auburn
facts.known: her escape from slavery in 1849; some 13 rescue missions into Maryland; the name "Moses"; her help to John Brown before the raid on Harpers Ferry; the Combahee River raid of 1863; her work for women's suffrage; the Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged

t: Born into slavery in Maryland and left with lifelong seizures and visions by an overseer's blow, Tubman escaped to Philadelphia in 1849 and went back again and again to bring out her family and others.

Known as "Moses", she rescued some 70 people in about 13 missions on the Underground Railroad, and in the Civil War she served the Union as a nurse, scout and spy, guiding the Combahee River raid of 1863.
She spent her last decades poor in Auburn, New York, campaigning for women's suffrage and caring for the old and needy, and after her death she became an American icon of courage and freedom.
dyk: Tubman began her escapes on Saturday evenings, because newspapers would not print runaway notices until Monday morning.
ev: Born Araminta Ross into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland
Escapes from slavery to Philadelphia, travelling by night with the help of the Underground Railroad
Guides her niece Kessiah and Kessiah's children to Philadelphia in the year of the Fugitive Slave Act
Leads her aging parents north to St. Catharines, Canada
Meets John Brown and helps him plan and recruit supporters for his raid on Harpers Ferry
Guides the Union raid on the Combahee River, which carries more than 750 enslaved people to freedom
Gives the keynote speech at the first conference of the National Federation of Afro-American Women
Dies of pneumonia in Auburn, New York, and is buried with semi-military honours

sections.early:
Harriet Tubman was born Araminta "Minty" Ross to enslaved parents, Harriet ("Rit") Green and Ben Ross, in Dorchester County, Maryland. As with many enslaved people, neither the year nor the place of her birth is known exactly: Tubman gave 1825, her death certificate 1815 and her gravestone 1820, while the historian Kate Larson's 2004 biography records 1822 from a midwife payment and other documents, and recent biographies accept March 1822 as most likely. Her maternal grandmother, Modesty, arrived on a slave ship from Africa. Edward Brodess, who enslaved Rit, sold three of her daughters, separating them from the family forever; when he tried to sell her youngest son, Moses, Rit hid him and threatened to split open the head of the first man to enter her house, and the sale was abandoned.

Hired out from the age of five or six, Tubman was whipped whenever the baby she minded cried, and carried the scars all her life. As an adolescent she was struck by a two-pound metal weight that an overseer threw at another enslaved man, which she said "broke my skull". She lay without medical care for two days and was comatose for weeks. Afterwards she suffered painful headaches and seizures, which Larson suggests may have been temporal lobe epilepsy and Clinton narcolepsy or cataplexy, and visions she took as revelations from God. Illiterate, she rejected white preachers' calls for obedience and found guidance in the Old Testament tales of deliverance.
sections.rise:
Around 1844 she married John Tubman, a free black man; any children of the marriage would have been enslaved, since a child took the mother's status. She changed her name from Araminta to Harriet, adopting her mother's name, though when is unclear. Later in the 1840s she paid a white attorney five dollars to look into her mother's status and learned that Atthow Pattison's will had provided for Rit and her children to be freed at 45, a stipulation the Pattison and Brodess families had ignored.

In 1849, ill again, she found that Edward Brodess was trying to sell her. She prayed for him to change his ways, then for God to kill him; a week later he died, and she expressed regret. His widow, Eliza, began to sell the people the family enslaved. On 17 September 1849 Tubman escaped with her brothers Ben and Henry, but the brothers had second thoughts and forced her to return with them. In October or November she left alone, singing a farewell song as a hint to a trusted fellow slave, Mary. She used the Underground Railroad, an informal network of free and enslaved black people, white abolitionists and other activists, many of them Quakers, and probably went along the Choptank River, through Delaware and into Pennsylvania, nearly 90 miles on foot by night, guided by the North Star. Of crossing into Pennsylvania she recalled: "I looked at my hands to see if I was the same person."
sections.deeds:
While Tubman worked odd jobs in Philadelphia, Congress passed the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which forced law enforcement officials even in free states to help capture people who had escaped slavery. In December 1850 she helped her niece Kessiah and Kessiah's children escape an auction in Cambridge, Maryland, and early the next year she brought out her youngest brother, Moses. From 1851 to 1862 she returned again and again to the Eastern Shore of Maryland, rescuing some 70 people in about 13 expeditions, among them her brothers Henry, Ben and Robert, and gave instructions to 50 to 60 others who escaped. She guided escapees on into British North America, and in 1857 led her parents to St. Catharines, Canada. Her efforts earned her the name "Moses".

She worked mostly in winter and began escapes on Saturday evenings, used disguises, sang versions of "Go Down Moses" as coded signals and carried a revolver. She later said she "never lost a passenger". In 1858 she met John Brown and helped him plan and recruit for his raid on Harpers Ferry.

In the Civil War she worked for the Union Army as a cook, nurse, scout and spy. In 1863 she led a band of scouts around Port Royal, South Carolina, and guided three steamboats of black soldiers under Colonel James Montgomery past mines on the Combahee River; the raid carried more than 750 formerly enslaved people away, and she is widely credited as the first woman to lead U.S. troops in an armed assault.
sections.opponents:
By the late 1850s Eastern Shore slaveholders were holding public meetings about the number of escapes, casting suspicion on free blacks and white abolitionists without knowing that "Minty" was responsible. A popular legend of a $40,000 reward for her capture is a manufactured figure, taken from an 1867 letter by the abolitionist Sallie Holley. Tubman threatened to shoot anyone who tried to turn back, since that would endanger the group, and once pointed her gun at a man's head and said "Go on or die". The historian Jonathan Chism argues that such stories reflect the extreme conditions of escape and raise ethical questions about leadership and survival, while noting that there is no evidence she killed anyone.

She condemned Abraham Lincoln for reprimanding General David Hunter, who had declared the "contrabands" of Port Royal free, and for his unwillingness to consider ending slavery. In 1865 a train conductor and other men forced her into a smoking car, injuring her, while white passengers cursed her. The government was slow to recognise her service: an 1874 bill to pay her $2,000 was defeated in the Senate, and when a soldier's pension was proposed in 1897 some members of Congress objected to paying a woman a full soldier's pension.

In 1859 she brought from Maryland an eight-year-old girl, Margaret, whom she called her niece; Margaret's daughter Alice called it a "kidnapping". Larson later found evidence that Margaret was the daughter of a free black couple, Isaac and Mary Woolford. Tubman's part in the Combahee raid has sometimes been exaggerated.
sections.last:
After the war Tubman returned to the farm in Fleming, beside Auburn, New York, that Frances Adeline Seward had sold her in 1859, and cared for her aging parents, relatives and boarders. For over three years of service she had received $200 in all, and her work for others kept her in constant poverty. On 18 March 1869 she married Nelson Davis, a veteran of the 8th United States Colored Infantry Regiment 22 years younger than she; they adopted a girl, Gertie, in 1874. Sarah Hopkins Bradford's authorized biography of 1869 brought her some $1,200. In 1873 swindlers who promised her a trunk of gold coins knocked her out with chloroform and stole her purse.

After Davis died in 1888 she was granted a widow's pension of $8 a month in 1895, and in 1899 Congress approved $20 a month, without acknowledging her as a scout and spy. In her later years she worked for women's suffrage alongside Susan B. Anthony and Emily Howland. Asked whether women ought to have the vote, she replied: "I suffered enough to believe it."

In 1896 she bought land beside her farm for a home for the aged, which the AME Zion Church took over in 1903 and opened in 1908, to her dismay with a $100 entrance fee. In the late 1890s a doctor in Boston operated on her skull. By 1911 she was so frail that she was admitted into the home named in her honour, and she died of pneumonia on 10 March 1913. She was buried at Fort Hill Cemetery in Auburn.
sections.legacy:
Widely known and respected in her lifetime, Tubman became an American icon after her death; by the 1980s she was one of American history's most famous figures. She inspired generations of African Americans struggling for equality and civil rights and has been praised by leaders across the political spectrum. Frederick Douglass, contrasting his public work with hers, wrote that "the midnight sky and the silent stars" had been the witnesses of her devotion to freedom.

She never wrote her own memoirs. Sarah Hopkins Bradford's Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman, which combined her recollections with press accounts and letters, is criticised by modern biographers for its artistic license and subjective point of view, though it gives insight into Tubman's view of her experiences; Bradford's revision of 1886, Harriet, the Moses of her People, hailed her as a latter-day Joan of Arc. Biographies based on original scholarship came from Jean Humez in 2003 and Kate Clifford Larson and Catherine Clinton in 2004, and Edda L. Fields-Black's 2024 study of the Combahee River Raid won the Pulitzer Prize for History.

National historical parks in Maryland and Auburn bear her name, and Canada designated her a National Historic Person. In 1978 she became the first African-American woman honoured on a U.S. postage stamp. Plans begun in 2016 to put her portrait on the twenty-dollar bill were said in 2026 to be no longer planned. In 2024 she was posthumously commissioned a brigadier general in the Maryland Army National Guard.

summary: Harriet Tubman (c. 1822–1913), born Araminta Ross into slavery in Maryland, escaped in 1849 and returned some 13 times to lead about 70 people to freedom on the Underground Railroad. In the Civil War she was a Union scout and spy who guided the Combahee River raid, and in old age she campaigned for women's suffrage.

notes: Birth: the article gives c. March 1822 (Larson's dating; Tubman gave 1825, her death certificate 1815, her gravestone 1820); start 1822, circa true.
The Combahee raid: the article's lead says it liberated 'more than 700' enslaved people, its raid section 'more than 750'; the profile follows the raid section.

Rescue years: the article says she returned 'from 1851 to 1862' but also that her last rescue mission was in November 1860, and quotes her as conductor 'for eight years'; the role fact says only '1850s' and the section keeps the article's 1851-1862 wording for the expeditions.
Bradford's Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman: the Later life section dates it 1869, the Historiography section 1868; 1869 is used in 'last', no year in 'legacy'.

The first-woman claim: the lead says 'the first woman to lead an armed military operation in the United States', the raid section 'the first woman to lead U.S. troops in an armed assault'; the latter is used.
Margaret's year: the article says shortly after Tubman acquired the farm in early 1859.
The 2026 remark on the twenty-dollar bill is given as a bare dated fact; the article names the Treasury secretary, left out here.

Left out for space: the Kessiah rescue in detail, the routes named to Wilbur Siebert in 1897, Thomas Garrett and William Still, the Fort Wagner battle and Robert Gould Shaw, the 1880 house fire, the artistic portrayals.
